demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it
I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.explanation: For trauma involving unexpected death of a loved one, repeated triggers centered on children (kids crying, being around children) are hard to explain unless the deceased was a child or the death specifically involved children; with no supporting memory, threat, or appraisal content linking the loss to children, this trigger pattern is clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: Avoiding sex is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The reported triggers and appraisals focus on grief/disconnection rather than bodily violation, intimacy threat, or sexual trauma themes, so this strategy appears to address a symptom domain absent elsewhere in the selected items.

Feeling 'like an object, not like a person' is more characteristic of interpersonal violation, coercion, or depersonalized trauma responses. In a bereavement profile, without corroborating memory, trigger, or strategy content suggesting objectification or dissociation, this appraisal is difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Triggers: Children Present: Being around children
issues.explanation: For traumatic bereavement, 'being around children' is not impossible as a trigger, but in this profile it lacks support from the other selected items. There are no memory, threat, or appraisal items linking the loss to children or parenting, so this trigger feels clinically unanchored relative to the rest of the profile.

'Avoid Sex' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the self-report. Sexual avoidance is more typically anchored to interpersonal/sexual trauma or marked contamination/intimacy themes, none of which are represented elsewhere in the selected triggers or appraisals for a bereavement presentation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person
issues.explanation: 'I feel like an object, not like a person' is poorly matched to unexpected death of a loved one in the absence of other humiliation, assault, or depersonalization-related content. It does not cohere well with the grief-linked triggers and appears disconnected from the stated maladaptive strategies and formulation.

vignette:
Sofia, a 38-year-old factory worker, had always thought of herself as someone who could handle whatever life threw at her. She had emigrated from Guatemala fifteen years ago, found steady work on an assembly line, and built a quiet but contented life. Then, two years ago, her younger brother Miguel was killed when a drunk driver ran a red light and slammed into his car. Sofia received the call from the hospital while she was on her lunch break; she could hear sirens wailing in the background of the caller's voice. By the time she arrived, he was already gone. The funeral was held three days later, and Sofia stood at the graveside feeling as though the earth had swallowed not just her brother but the person she used to be.

In the weeks that followed, Sofia began to notice that certain sounds could stop her cold. Every time an ambulance or police car passed the factory floor-the building was near a major intersection-she would freeze, her hands trembling over the circuit boards she was assembling. The low hum of machinery became a constant backdrop, but a siren cut through it like a blade. She started taking a different route to work, one that avoided the fire station entirely, but even then, there was no guarantee. At home, she kept the television volume low and the windows shut. She stopped answering her phone when she saw it was her sister, because her sister inevitably brought up Miguel: a memory, a photo, a question about how Sofia was coping. Any mention of someone losing a loved one-a coworker mentioning a friend whose mother had died, a news story about a family in mourning-sent a sharp spike of anxiety through her chest. She stopped attending family gatherings entirely, afraid that someone would suggest visiting the cemetery, or that her mother would break down and Sofia would have to witness it again.

The thought of the funeral itself, of the raw earth and the flowers and the rows of chairs, became so unbearable that she made a rule for herself: she would never set foot in a cemetery again. She also avoided any conversation that turned toward grief, steering the topic elsewhere or excusing herself to the bathroom. Yet she could not stop her mind from returning to that day. Over and over, she replayed the details of the accident: which road Miguel had taken, what time he left work, whether she could have called him to delay him by five minutes. She went over the hospital phone call again and again, trying to find a different meaning, a different outcome. The rumination left her exhausted, and yet she could not let it go. She began asking her coworkers, her sister, even the cashier at the grocery store, "Do I seem okay to you? Am I acting normal?" She needed someone to confirm that she was still functioning, because inside she felt shattered.

Sofia had come to believe that she no longer belonged anywhere. She used to be the person who laughed easily, who organized the factory's holiday potlucks, who visited her mother every Sunday. Now she felt like an impostor in her own life. At work, she kept her head down and spoke only when necessary. Her supervisor had already pulled her aside twice to ask if everything was all right; she gave vague answers. She had lost interest in the TV shows she used to enjoy, in cooking, in texting her friends. When she looked at herself in the mirror, she saw someone hollow. She was certain that the trauma had destroyed any chance of future happiness. How could she ever be the person she was before, when every step forward felt like walking on broken glass?

What finally brought her to seek help was a note from her supervisor warning that her absences and errors on the line were becoming a problem. Sofia had missed three shifts in the past month, each time because a siren had triggered a panic attack that left her unable to leave the house. She knew she was risking her job, the one stable thing she still had. She made an appointment at a community mental health clinic, terrified that the therapist would confirm she was beyond repair, but also hoping-almost against hope-that somewhere inside her, the person she used to be might still exist.
